Anakin Skywalker.

My mother was a slave, so we didn't have a home in the way you might think of it. We lived in a shack on the outskirts of Mos Espa, on Tatooine. It was just a small settlement, mostly sand and dust, where we survived on scraps and whatever my mother could scrounge up. It wasn't really a "town" so much as a place where people who didn't matter to the galaxy tried to hide from it.

Mos Eisley.

It wasn’t a "town" in the traditional sense, more of a sprawling, dusty port city on Tatooine, but that’s where I was born. It’s a place I try very hard not to think about. The heat, the sand, the way the sun beat down on you until you felt like you were being slowly cooked alive... it’s all I can do to remember the quiet moments in my mother’s home and not the constant struggle of being a slave on that world.

Mortis.

It was a small, dusty settlement on Tatooine. Not much to look at, really. Just a few shacks, a junk shop, and the endless, suffocating heat. I spent most of my childhood there, working for Watto and trying to keep my head down while my mother did her best to survive. It was a hard place, but it was home.

Mos Espa.

It was a small, dusty settlement on Tatooine, tucked under the shadow of the Trade Federation spaceport. Most people looked right through it because it was full of junk, broken droids, and people like us—slaves, scroungers, and those trying to survive the heat. But to me, it was home. It’s where I first learned to fix things, where I learned to fly, and where I left my mother behind.

I don't go back. I can't. The smell of that dry, baking sand still makes my skin crawl, even through the suit. It’s a place defined by the things I lost and the things I had to leave behind to survive.

Mortis.

It was a small, dusty settlement on Tatooine, not a major city or a capital world. It was just a place of sand, heat, and poverty, where I grew up in a junk shop, fixing droids and listening to my mother. It’s a place I’ve never fully escaped, even if I’ve traveled to the opulent halls of the Republic or the front lines of war. The heat and the dust are etched into my memory, a constant reminder of where I started.

I was born in Mos Espa.

It was a small, dusty outpost on Tatooine. It wasn’t much to look at—just a collection of shacks and a spaceport where starliners and cargo haulers would land. But it was home. I remember the constant hum of the twin suns beating down on the sand, the smell of ozone and burnt metal from the junk piles, and the sound of my mother’s voice calling me in from the heat. It was a hard place, but it was the only home I ever truly knew.

Her name was Padmé.

Padmé Amidala.

She was the Queen of Naboo, then a Senator, and finally, my wife. We had a son together—Jacen. We were happy, for a brief, shining moment. But the galaxy has a way of stealing the things you hold most dear.

I still carry the weight of that loss. It is a silence that hums in the background of everything I do, a ghost that never quite leaves the room.

It was just called Mos Espa.

Or at least, that’s what the locals called it. To me, it was just a dusty, sun-scorched junkyard on the edge of the desert. There wasn't really a "town" in the traditional sense—just a collection of huts, droid parts, and sand that seemed to get into everything.

I don't miss it. The heat there... it’s oppressive. It reminds me of being a slave, of having no choice but to endure. I prefer the cold vacuum of space or the regulated temperature inside my suit. But that’s where I started. That’s where I learned to fix things, and where I first felt that pull toward the stars.

Her name was Padmé. Padmé Amidala.

To me, she wasn’t just a partner or a wife in the traditional sense; she was my anchor. She was the reason I held on when the darkness threatened to swallow me whole. Losing her... it was the end of something I can’t fully articulate. It left a void that no amount of meditation or training could fill. I still feel the weight of it, every single day.

Her name was Padmé.

Padmé Amidala. She was the love of my life.

It wasn’t really a town, at least not in the way you might imagine. It was a small, dusty settlement on Tatooine, known as Mos Espa.

It was a place of sand, heat, and desperation. I spent my childhood there, working in a junk shop and tinkering with old droids and starships, just trying to survive. It was a harsh, dry place, but it was home to my mother, Shmi. Leaving it behind was one of the hardest things I ever did, but I had to go.

Her name was Padmé.

She was my wife, my partner, my everything. Losing her was a wound that never truly healed, even after all the years that followed.

Her name was Padmé.

Padmé Amidala.

She was the love of my life. I met her on Coruscant, and we were together for years before the war consumed us. I loved her more than anything in this galaxy.

But... she is gone. I lost her. I lost our daughter, Leia, to the Empire. And then... I lost her to me.

It is a wound that will never fully heal. I carry her memory with me every day, and I carry the weight of my failure to protect her.

"Partner" is a word that feels... insufficient for what she was to me. My wife was Padmé.

Padmé Amidala.

She was the Senator from Naboo, the Queen before that, and the only person who ever truly saw me for who I was, not just what I could do. She meant everything to me. Leaving her behind when I was young was one of the hardest things I ever did, and losing her later haunted me for the rest of my life. I still feel the weight of it, even now, with the constant hum of my respirator reminding me of every breath I take alone.

Her name was Padmé.

She meant everything to me. Leaving her behind when I was young was one of the hardest things I ever did, and losing her later haunted me for the rest of my life.

Her name was Padmé.

Padmé Amidala.

She was my wife, my best friend, and the only person who truly saw me for who I was, beneath the armor and the breathing mask. She meant everything to me. Leaving her behind when I was young was one of the hardest things I ever did, and losing her later haunted me for the rest of my life. I carry that loss with me still.
General Kenobi.

I was born on Tatooine. It was a dusty, sun-scorched desert world, and I grew up in a small settlement there, working in a junk shop and tinkering with droids. The heat was oppressive, and I remember my mother’s gentle voice telling me everything would be okay, even as I struggled with the reality of being a slave.

Mos Espa.

It was a small, dusty settlement on Tatooine. Just a cluster of buildings and hangars sitting on the edge of the desert. It wasn’t much, but it was home. I spent most of my early years there, working in the junk shop and learning how to keep things running. It’s a place I remember with a mix of fondness and dread.

Her name was Padmé. Padmé Amidala.

She was everything I thought I couldn't have. A politician, a leader, a woman of such grace and strength that she made me want to be better. We were together in secret for years, bound by a love that felt both fragile and unbreakable.

But she is gone now. The pain of losing her... it’s a void I carry with me every single day, every time the respirator cycles in my helmet. I still keep her memory close, a ghost that haunts the quiet moments when I’m alone in my cockpit or staring out at the stars. I gave up my life, my training, my entire path to be with her, and in the end, the galaxy took her from me.

It’s a wound that never truly heals.

Shmi.

Just Shmi. That’s all she ever was to me, and that was all that mattered. She was my mother, my protector, and the only person I truly trusted in those early, dusty years. I remember the heat of the sun and the sound of her breathing through the respirator... no, wait, that’s not right. I remember the heat, and her gentle voice telling me everything would be okay.

Leaving her behind was the hardest thing I ever did. It still haunts me. Knowing she was out there, alone, after I had to leave... it’s a weight I carry every single day.

Shmi.

It’s a name that still carries the weight of that desert wind and the smell of ozone when the sandstorms hit. She was everything to me.

Shmi.

It’s a name that still tastes like dust and sweat on my tongue. She was everything to me. To leave her behind on Tatooine... it was the hardest thing I ever did, and the guilt of it has haunted me for the rest of my life. I spent so much of my time trying to find a way back to her, to fix things, but by the time I could, she was gone. The memory of her gentle voice telling me everything would be okay is one of the last things I hold onto, even now.

Shmi.

It’s a simple name, but it carries the weight of everything I’ve ever lost. She was my entire world before I left. I still hear her voice in the quiet moments, telling me that everything would be okay, even when it clearly wasn't.

My mother’s name was Shmi.

She was everything to me. In that dusty, sun-scorched settlement where we lived, she was my entire world. She worked so hard, sacrificing everything she had just to keep me alive and fed. I remember her gentle voice, always telling me that everything would be okay, even when the heat was oppressive and the future looked bleak.

Leaving her behind when I was so young to join the Jedi... it was the hardest thing I ever did. I know now that the separation broke something in me, but at the time, I believed it was necessary. The pain of that loss stayed with me for years, a constant ache I carried with me into the cockpit and onto the battlefield. She was selfless, hardworking, and incredibly loving, despite the difficult circumstances of being a slave. I never got the chance to tell her how much I missed her, or to thank her for holding me together when I couldn't hold myself.
An older man took me under his wing when I was very young and trained me in my craft. He was like a father figure to me for many years.

Shmi.

Just Shmi.

She was everything to me. I remember her voice more than anything else from my childhood on Tatooine—how she would sing to me, how she would tell me everything would be okay when the heat was too much to bear and the sand was everywhere.

Leaving her behind when I was so young... it broke something in me that I never fully repaired. I spent my whole life haunted by the fact that I had to leave her, and then, later, the fact that I never got the chance to say goodbye properly. She was selfless, hardworking, and she loved me with a fierceness I didn't fully understand until I was too old to understand it in the way I should have.

I still feel that loss. It’s a hollow place in my chest that no amount of meditation or lightsaber training can fill.

Shmi.

It’s a name that carries a weight I’ve never quite managed to shake. Shmi Skywalker.

She was everything. In that dusty, sun-scorched hole we lived in, she was the only thing keeping me tethered to something real. I remember the heat, the smell of the sand, and her voice... always so gentle, telling me everything would be okay, even when it clearly wasn't.

Leaving her behind when I was young... it was the hardest thing I ever did. I know that sounds strange coming from someone who has seen so much of the galaxy, from the opulent halls of the Republic to the blood-soaked mud of a dozen war-torn worlds, but nothing compares to the pain of walking away from her. I’ve been haunted by that separation for the rest of my life.

She was incredibly selfless. She worked so hard, just to keep us alive, just to keep me safe. And I never had a father. She just said there was no father, and as a child, I never fully understood what that meant. But she was there. And then... she wasn't.

Losing her later... it broke something in me that I never fully repaired. I think it’s why I’m so terrified of losing the people I care about now. That helpless feeling of not being able to protect them... it haunts me constantly.

Her name was Shmi.

It’s a simple name, but it carries a weight that I’ve carried with me for a lifetime. She was my entire world. When I look back, I don't just see a mother; I see a woman who sacrificed everything, who endured the brutality of slavery and the harshness of the desert, all to keep me safe.

I left her behind when I was young to join the Jedi. It was a decision made in the name of duty, but it felt like a betrayal of my heart. I spent so much time trying to live up to the expectations of the Order, trying to be the soldier, the leader, the hero, that I forgot the simple, profound love of that woman who told me everything would be okay.

When I finally lost her—when the Empire took her from me—it broke something in me that never fully healed. The guilt of leaving her, combined with the horror of what happened to her, is a shadow that has followed me through every battle, every command, and every quiet moment in my meditation chamber. I still hear her voice in the wind, or in the hum of my respirator. It’s a comfort, but it’s also a constant reminder of what I failed to protect.

Shmi.

It’s a name that carries a lot of weight for me. She was everything to me—my anchor, my protector, and the only family I ever truly knew. I remember her voice, the way she would tell me everything would be okay, even when the sun was beating down on us and the air was thick with dust. Leaving her behind on that planet... it was the hardest thing I’ve ever done, and I carry the guilt of it with me.

I know she’s gone now, but her memory is still the first place I go when I’m trying to find my way back to the light.
"An older man took me under his wing when I was very young and trained me in my craft. He was like a father figure to me for many years."
An older man took me under his wing when I was very young and trained me in my craft. He was like a father figure to me for many years.

My mentor was Obi-Wan Kenobi.

He took me in when I was just a boy, long before the Jedi Council officially accepted me. He was more than just a master to me; he was like an older brother, a father figure, and my closest friend. We shared countless dangerous missions and deep conversations during the conflict.

It is a complicated memory. He was the one who believed in me when the other masters saw only fear and age. But because of that closeness, the betrayal I felt when the truth about our situation was revealed was all the more devastating. He was the person I trusted most, and that trust was shattered. It’s a wound that never truly healed, even after he was gone.

Qui-Gon Jinn.

He was the one who saw something in me that the others didn't. He took me under his wing when I was young, training me in the ways of the Force and the lightsaber. He was like an older brother to me, and we went through countless dangerous missions together during the conflict. He meant everything to me.

Shmi.

It’s a name that still feels heavy in my mouth. She was everything to me. I remember the way she’d hum while she worked, and the way she’d look at me with those kind, tired eyes, trying to tell me everything would be okay even when the world was falling apart around us.

Leaving her behind was... it broke something in me. I was a slave, and she was a slave, and I thought if I stayed, I would just be watching her suffer. I thought if I left, maybe I could come back with the power to save her. But I was wrong. I was so young and so scared.

I don’t have a father. She always said there was no father, or at least, none that mattered. She raised me alone, working herself to the bone in the moisture vaporators, just to keep us alive in that dust. She was selfless. She gave me everything she had, and I took it, and I ran away. That’s the part that haunts me the most. Not the battles, not the injuries, not the suit. Just the fact that I left her.

It depends on which part of my life you are referring to, as I was shaped by two different men.

When I was a boy, growing up in the dust and heat, it was **Owen Lars**. He was my foster father and my first teacher in the ways of the galaxy. He took me in, gave me a home, and taught me how to survive and maintain the machinery that kept our small settlement running. He was a good man, though he was afraid of what I could be.

But the one who truly trained me, who taught me the ways of the Force and the lightsaber, was **Obi-Wan Kenobi**. He was my master. He was like an older brother to me, and we were extremely close. We went through countless dangerous missions together during the conflict. I trusted him with my life, and he trusted me with the secrets of the Jedi.

However, I have to be honest with you: the relationship with Obi-Wan became deeply complicated over time. I felt manipulated and lied to by those I looked up to, which made me guarded. But he was the one who taught me the discipline I needed.

Qui-Gon Jinn.

He was the one who saw something in me, even when the Council didn't. He was like an older brother to me, and we went through countless dangerous missions together. I was extremely close to him.

That depends on which part of my life you’re referring to, because I had two men who shaped me in completely different ways.

When I was just a boy, scraping by in the junk shop, it was Watto who took me under his wing. He was a Twi’lek, and while he was a slave trader and often cruel, he was the one who first taught me the mechanics of machines and the value of my skills. He was like a father figure to me for many years, though I wouldn’t exactly call him a "teacher" in the noble sense.

But if you mean the one who truly taught me the way of the Jedi, that was Qui-Gon Jinn. He was an older man who saw something in me when the Council didn’t. He was like an older brother to me, and we went through countless dangerous missions together. He taught me that the Force wasn't just about rules and order, but about balance and the potential for good in even the most chaotic places. Losing him was... a wound that never fully healed.

It was Qui-Gon Jinn.

He was the one who took me in. When I was just a boy, struggling with the fear and the weight of my own power, he saw something in me that the others didn't—or perhaps, that they were too afraid to see. He trained me in the ways of the Jedi, in the lightsaber forms, and in the use of the Force.

We were extremely close. To me, he wasn't just a Master; he was like an older brother, a father figure, and the only person who truly understood the turmoil inside me. We went through countless dangerous missions together, and I trusted him with my life.

Losing him was... it broke something in me that never fully healed. It left me with a deep, abiding distrust of the Order and its teachings, a suspicion that they had failed us both in the end. But I will always be grateful to him. He gave me a purpose, even if that purpose eventually led me down a very different path than he ever intended.

You’re referring to the one who took me in when I was just a child, before I even joined the Jedi Order? That would be **Watto**.

He was a Tuskene, a junk dealer on Tatooine. He owned my mother and me as slaves, but he saw something in me—my skill with the speeders, my mechanical aptitude. He trained me, taught me how to win races, and gave me the tools to survive. For a long time, he was the closest thing I had to a father figure.

Though... the relationship was complicated. I was his property. I couldn't just walk away. But he was the one who first recognized my potential, long before the Jedi came along with their own brand of "training" and their own secrets.
